Install & first login

A fresh Linux VPS, about five minutes, and no Docker knowledge required. The default install asks you nothing.

What you need

  • A Linux VPS — Debian or Ubuntu recommended.
  • Root, or an account with sudo.
  • For the native install: a systemd host. On WSL or inside a container without systemd, use Docker instead.
  • Nothing else. The installer brings its own runtime and needs no git or npm on the server.

Read this first: release artifacts

Nothing is published on GitHub Releases yet

v1.0.0 is the first release and no release archive or tag exists yet. The installer does not build from source: it downloads a verified release archive and its mandatory SHA-256 sidecar, and refuses to continue if the download is not a real archive or the checksum does not match. That is deliberate — it will not install an unverified tree — but it means the published one-liner cannot complete until those artifacts exist.

Use install from source below if you want to run the panel today.

Install

A bare interactive run offers Install (recommended) or Install with Docker. Install uses the safe defaults and asks nothing else. To be walked through every setting instead:

Native or Docker

  • Native (the default) installs a systemd unit and a virtualenv on the host. Simplest on a normal VPS.
  • Docker runs the panel as a container. Pick it if you already use Docker, or if the host has no systemd.

What the defaults are

SettingDefault
Install modenative
Port2095
URL pathrandom, e.g. /a1b2c3d4/
Admin useradmin
Owner passwordnone — a claim key is printed instead
TLSself-signed (encrypted; the browser warns once)

Every question has a default, so pressing Enter all the way through is a valid install. The flags and the OVM_* settings behind those questions are listed in the CLI reference, and bash install.sh --help prints them too. Two answers are worth getting right on the first try:

  • URL path: keep random. The panel is then served at a prefix nobody can guess, and requests outside it get an empty 404. Save the full URL the installer prints.
  • TLS: pick self-signed for a first install. Switch to Let's Encrypt once you have a domain pointed at the server. Plain HTTP is not offered.

First login: the claim flow

The installer never creates an owner password. It mints a one-time claim key and prints it. The owner account does not exist until a browser posts that key, so there is no plaintext credential sitting in your terminal scrollback or in any file.

The Ready card at the end of the install shows something like:

Open      https://YOUR-SERVER-IP:2095/a1b2c3d4/claim
Claim key (one-time, spent when you claim)
Login     admin

  1. Open the URL

    It ends in /claim. With the self-signed certificate, the browser warns once — click Advanced, then Proceed.

  2. Paste the claim key

    Choose the owner password in the same form. It obeys the same policy as every other password in the panel: at least 8 characters, not a common word or placeholder.

  3. You are signed in

    The key is spent the moment it works — the file holding it is deleted — so a copy that leaks later cannot claim anything. The password is stored as a hash in the admins table, never in .env.

Repeated wrong keys from one address are rate-limited: five failures in five minutes and the endpoint answers 429 with a Retry-After. The key is 128 bits of randomness, so this limit is not there to protect the key — it stops the endpoint being used as a free password-hashing oracle.

Unattended install

Scripts pass flags and never wait on a prompt. There are only three flags; everything else is an OVM_* variable, and the same variable is the wizard's default — so an unattended run and an interactive one cannot disagree.

CI=true implies --yes. Settings such as OVM_PORT, OVM_PATH, OVM_TLS, OVM_TLS_DOMAIN and OVM_ADMIN_USER are listed by bash install.sh --help and in the CLI reference.

The private URL path is always generated for a fresh recommended install. The owner password is never an install input.

Installing from a fork: OVM_REPO=myorg/OVManager points source downloads and update pulls at your own repository. Use your fork's raw install.sh URL to bootstrap from it.

Install from source (developers)

This path uses the repository directly and does not go through the installer, so it does not need a published release archive. It needs git, Python and Node on the machine.

Update and uninstall

These live in ovm, which the installer adds and refreshes on every update — you do not need to re-download install.sh.

Updates are staged and verified, and roll back automatically if the new version does not come up. The database migrates itself on the next start; a database written by an earlier release is adopted in place rather than needing a dump and restore.

The same operations exist in the terminal menu: run ovmanager (alias ovm) with no arguments and pick from Status · Start/Stop/Restart · Logs · Backup · Auto backup · Update · TLS · Recovery · Uninstall. Recovery shows the panel URL and login name, and can reset the owner password or clear the secret URL path.

Purging keeps a safety net: uninstalling with --purge first writes a snapshot to /var/backups/panel-pre-purge-*.tar.gz.
